title: Kaboom

jokes.text: Credit card fraud reveals someone bought both Netflix AND Blockbuster Online simultaneously
jokes.setup: A credit card company is reading back suspicious charges to confirm fraud
jokes.punchline: $20 to Netflix, $20 to Blockbuster Online — 'Both?' — the absurdity that someone paid for two competing services at once signals this is the cardholder herself
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of paying for competing services, and the dawning realization these aren't fraudulent charges at all. The single-word reaction 'Both?' is perfectly economical. Strong character integration — this over-prepared, can't-say-no-to-anything personality is quintessentially Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Credit Card Representative
dialogue.line: We've flagged some suspicious charges on your account. Multiple streaming services in a single month?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Those aren't suspicious. I have Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, HBO Max, and Amazon Prime.

dialogue.speaker: Credit Card Representative
dialogue.line: Ma'am, that's five different services. Most people just pick one.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Most people are sheep. I like to keep my options open so I can hate all of them equally.

jokes.text: I needed all 11 discs of Gossip Girl at the same time.
jokes.setup: The question hangs: why would anyone pay for both Netflix and Blockbuster?
jokes.punchline: She needed 11 discs of Gossip Girl simultaneously — an obsessive, impractical answer delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '11 discs' is what elevates this above a generic 'I watch too much TV' joke. Leslie's earnestness makes it a character reveal as much as a punchline. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have Netflix and Blockbuster because sometimes I need to watch all the discs at the same time.

jokes.text: $120 in tuition to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.
jokes.setup: We're hearing a list of supposedly fraudulent charges on the credit card
jokes.punchline: Hogwarts tuition — a fictional school — listed as a real charge, escalating the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Good absurdist escalation in the running list of charges. The real-world specificity of '$120 in tuition' paired with an obviously fictional school creates a nice incongruity. Slightly reliant on the Harry Potter reference as a pop-culture crutch.

dialogue.speaker: Credit Card Representative
dialogue.line: There's a charge here for Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry for $3,500.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's my tuition.

dialogue.speaker: Credit Card Representative
dialogue.line: Ma'am, Hogwarts isn't real.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know that. But the tuition is.

jokes.text: They give you a little wand and a diploma, it's fun.
jokes.setup: Hogwarts tuition was flagged as a suspicious charge
jokes.punchline: Leslie defends it with cheery matter-of-factness — the wand and diploma justify the price
jokes.explanation: 'It's fun' as justification for paying tuition to a fictional wizard school is a perfect Leslie line. The cheerful consumer-satisfaction framing is hilarious. Strong character integration — only Leslie would defend this so earnestly. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I got a 3.8 GPA at Hogwarts. I was in Ravenclaw. I wrote my thesis on the mating habits of hippogriffs.

jokes.text: What'd you major in? Potions.
jokes.setup: The credit card rep asks a follow-up about Leslie's Hogwarts 'diploma' — treating it as real
jokes.punchline: Potions — a specific, perfectly chosen answer that commits fully to the bit
jokes.explanation: The beauty here is that both parties are now playing the fiction straight. 'Potions' is the ideal Harry Potter-specific answer — not 'magic' or something generic, but the actual course name. Perfect economy. The credit card rep asking a follow-up is an unexpected second beat that rewards the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Credit Card Representative
dialogue.line: We've also got charges for Butt Pucker Lip Gloss, Booty Sweat Energy Drink, and a product called Colon Blow Cereal.

jokes.text: Leslie takes herself off speakerphone after the Hogwarts exchange
jokes.setup: Coworkers have been listening to the embarrassing credit card call on speakerphone
jokes.punchline: Only NOW — after the wand-and-diploma and Potions major — does Leslie decide to take it off speakerphone
jokes.explanation: The comedic timing of when she removes the speakerphone is the joke — she was fine with the absurd charges being public, but this belated discretion signals a self-awareness she doesn't fully possess. Subtle but effective.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait, no, I didn't mean— okay, fine, yes, I bought them. But I'm hanging up now.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And don't you dare tell anyone I'm keeping them. Especially not Jerry.

jokes.text: I'm gonna take you off speakerphone. Go ahead.
jokes.setup: The credit card charges have been escalating in absurdity with colleagues listening
jokes.punchline: Realizing her colleagues are hearing this, Leslie removes the speakerphone — implicitly acknowledging these are her charges all along
jokes.explanation: A beautifully understated pivot. The act of taking it off speaker IS the confession without ever saying so. Works as character comedy and a visual/implied-action beat. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's Daniel Craig. For back support.

jokes.text: Jessica Simpson clip-in hair extensions. I wore those once.
jokes.setup: More charges being read on the now-private call, which we can still hear
jokes.punchline: Leslie's casual 'I wore those once' — past tense, implying ownership — is the confirmation she bought them
jokes.explanation: Decent escalation beat in the running gag, but less clever than the Hogwarts material. The punchline mechanism (self-incrimination) is the same as the other charges, starting to feel repetitive.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: High five!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't trust it. It's too fast.

jokes.text: Man-Pillow, the pillow shaped like a man. Also something called 'bucket of cake'.
jokes.setup: The list of suspicious charges continues escalating
jokes.punchline: 'Bucket of cake' — an object that sounds ridiculous but is also immediately understandable and somehow perfect as a Leslie Knope purchase
jokes.explanation: 'Bucket of cake' is a brilliantly specific absurdist image — not a slice, not a cake, a BUCKET of cake. The Man-Pillow is also funny on its own, but 'bucket of cake' is the sharper joke. Two distinct laughs packed into one exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This playground is going to be used by all kinds of kids. Jocks, nerds, preps, goths, sluts...

jokes.text: I think someone stole my credit card so cancel it. Do you wanna hear what else they purchased? Don't refund anything. Just cancel the credit card and we'll all go on with our lives.
jokes.setup: Leslie realizes she's heard enough to implicate herself
jokes.punchline: Her solution: cancel the card so they can't tell her anything more — not to dispute fraud, but to stop the list. 'Don't refund anything' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff for the entire cold open bit. 'Don't refund anything' is the perfect button — it fully concedes all the charges without ever admitting guilt. The structure is excellent: setup, escalation, and then a satisfying landing that subverts the fraud investigation framing entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: He only volunteers for the free food

jokes.text: What does a man-pillow look like? Daniel Craig. It's for my lower back.
jokes.setup: After Leslie hangs up, a colleague asks what a Man-Pillow looks like
jokes.punchline: Daniel Craig — then 'It's for my lower back' as a defensive afterthought
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff for the Man-Pillow joke. 'Daniel Craig' is perfect specificity — not just 'a handsome man' but a specific, ultra-fit movie star. The follow-up 'It's for my lower back' is a classic Leslie defensive justification that fools nobody. Excellent economy and structure. One of the episode's better jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I volunteered at a suicide prevention hotline. The catering was terrible. I mean, if you're already thinking about ending it all, the last thing you need is a sad chicken salad sandwich.

jokes.text: We're all volunteering for Kaboom! A service organization that says it builds a playground in a day. High five. I never trust anything that quickly. That's why I don't eat minute rice.
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically explains the Kaboom! organization's promise to build a playground in a day
jokes.punchline: Ron's skepticism is anchored in minute rice — an absurdly mundane comparison that perfectly encapsulates his distrust of anything expedient
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'That's why I don't eat minute rice' is a near-perfect Ron Swanson line: it's anti-government, anti-modern convenience, rooted in his worldview, and utterly unexpected. The specificity of minute rice as his proof point is genius — it says everything about who Ron is in seven words. Easily quotable and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You live in a pit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I live indoors. That's something.

jokes.text: Not if you have the kaboom spirit. You can look at a problem and you can either go 'This is a problem', or you can kaboom! Blow it up and turn it into something great.
jokes.setup: Leslie is impressed by the one-day turnaround; Keith explains the Kaboom philosophy
jokes.punchline: The Kaboom philosophy is circular and content-free — it's just saying 'kaboom' at problems
jokes.explanation: Keith as an over-enthusiastic motivational-speak character is a reliable comedic archetype. The joke is the vacuousness of the 'philosophy.' Functional but not exceptional — the target (motivational speaker nonsense) is well-worn territory.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have to go help with playground construction.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That sounds like fun.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're gonna be working with long, hard wood all day. Really getting our hands dirty. Lots of hard thrusting motions.

jokes.text: Fat kids, skinny kids, brainiacs, sluts, the gay drama kids, goths, jocks, the alternative crowd.
jokes.setup: Keith is giving an inspirational speech about all the kids who will enjoy this playground
jokes.punchline: The list starts normal (fat kids, skinny kids) then abruptly includes 'sluts' mid-inspirational-speech, then continues as if nothing happened
jokes.explanation: A classic list-subversion joke. The riff on the 'Picky Eater' song structure is recognizable but the insertion of 'sluts' into an inspirational playground speech is unexpected and dark enough to earn a real laugh. Keith remains oblivious, which is the key to it working.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I found this remote control at the construction site. Let me try something.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Points remote at Jerry. You there, freeze!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Now dance. Dance for me, puppet man. I control the remote, you control the dance. It rhymes, it's science.

jokes.text: The key to volunteering? A lot of pockets. For putting all the food in. The red cross has amazing cookies. I go there all the time. Meals on wheels was a bonanza. Suicide hotline, surprisingly lame spread.
jokes.setup: Tom explains his approach to volunteering
jokes.punchline: His entire motivation is the free food — culminating in 'Suicide hotline, surprisingly lame spread' as a perfectly dark button
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. The buildup through Red Cross and Meals on Wheels sets a pattern, and the suicide hotline punchline is perfectly dark without being cruel — it's about the food, not the callers. 'Surprisingly lame spread' is the killer phrase. Strong Tom character integration: self-serving, shallow, oblivious to how he sounds. One of the episode's standout jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you had ONE job. One job! Do you know how many people work in this office? Twelve. Twelve people, and somehow you managed to mess up the one thing that affects all of us. The copy machine. THE COPY MACHINE, Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I just pressed the wrong button—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wrong button? WRONG BUTTON?! Do you understand the butterfly effect, Jerry? One small action can have massive consequences. You pressed that button, and now we live in a world where nobody can copy anything. Nobody. That's not a world I want to live in, Jerry. That's not the world our forefathers died for.

jokes.text: Thought I'd give back to those less fortunate than myself. You live in a pit. Not anymore. Living with the drummer of my band. Living indoors. Pretty cool. Not to brag. Kinda hard not to.
jokes.setup: Andy says he's giving back to those less fortunate — Ann points out he lives in a pit
jokes.punchline: He's already moved out to the drummer's place; 'living indoors — pretty cool, not to brag, kinda hard not to' presents indoor living as an achievement worthy of boasting
jokes.explanation: Andy bragging about living indoors is a perfect character joke — it recontextualizes the extraordinarily low bar of his life circumstances as something brag-worthy. 'Not to brag. Kinda hard not to.' is a great button. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everyone, take out your doing caps.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I thought you meant condoms.

jokes.text: Me and an old Asian lady are double-teaming some monkey bars, so.
jokes.setup: Andy explains he has to go back to the playground build
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'double-teaming some monkey bars' paired with the specificity of 'old Asian lady' is wonderfully surreal and innocent
jokes.explanation: The double entendre in 'double-teaming' is clearly unintentional on Andy's part, which is key to the joke. His obliviousness is the punchline. The specificity adds a nice visual absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to move faster than a slug. Actually, let me rephrase that. I need to move faster than a slug on quaaludes. No wait—faster than a slug on quaaludes riding a very apathetic sloth. Hmm, or a slug on quaaludes riding a sloth that's also on quaaludes, but the sloth took twice as much because it's bigger. Actually, a slug on quaaludes riding a sloth on quaaludes while both are underwater in a vat of molasses during a solar eclipse.

jokes.text: I got a remote control and I'm controlling you. Go faster! 'Go faster, Ron's the master.'
jokes.setup: Ron, the hyper-masculine anti-government libertarian, is supposed to be building a playground
jokes.punchline: He has commandeered a child's remote control toy and is bossing a child around with a made-up rhyme, completely absorbed
jokes.explanation: The unexpected softness of Ron enjoying a toy is a great visual reveal. The self-composed rhyme 'Go faster, Ron's the master' is delightful — it suggests he's been at this for a while. Perfect character comedy: Ron is skeptical of everything except things that amuse him personally. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Would you break the rules to get things done?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes. I would kill someone.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I meant like, bend the rules.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh. No, of course not.

jokes.text: Take a man kabooming, he kabooms for a day. But you teach a man how to kaboom... Kaboom! Kaboom!
jokes.setup: Keith is saying goodbye and giving a final inspirational send-off
jokes.punchline: He mangles 'give a man a fish' into a kaboom-ified version with no logical payoff — just more kabooms
jokes.explanation: The running joke of Keith kabooming everything reaches a nice peak with the corrupted proverb. The trailing off into just more 'kabooms' is the right punchline — the philosophy is entirely self-referential. Good structure for what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: You should be bold. Don't ask permission.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Can I ask you something? Do I have your permission to not ask permission?

jokes.text: I could prep, like, 1,000 diagnostic tests. In an hour! That's the spirit.
jokes.setup: Everyone is pumped up on the Kaboom spirit; people are sharing what they'll do with this energy
jokes.punchline: Ann's specific medical ambition is hilariously mundane and task-oriented compared to the inspirational context — and Keith enthusiastically validates it
jokes.explanation: A competent joke about enthusiasm misapplied to ordinary tasks. Not particularly original but serves the scene's rhythmic function.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're going to rent some equipment that comes with an operator.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you're renting people?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That sounds like an escort service.

jokes.text: There's something I wish I could kaboom. Well, we are. It's just a slow boom. A slower, more deliberate kaboom.
jokes.setup: They're looking at the pit — Leslie wants to fill it in like Kaboom builds playgrounds
jokes.punchline: Mark's reframe of their government process as 'a slower, more deliberate kaboom' is perfectly dry
jokes.explanation: Good bureaucratic irony. The phrase 'slower, more deliberate kaboom' neatly captures the futility of government red tape while subverting the episode's central catchword. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, you want to know about my prom night? Well, let me tell you, it involved a backhoe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A backhoe?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, my date's dad had one. We went to the construction site, and she gave me a backhoe all night long.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Back massages. She just really liked giving back massages. Her hands were magic.

jokes.text: Jerry, did you use permanent marker again? I'm sorry, guys... Forget it. Let's all pretend Jerry wasn't born.
jokes.setup: The team is trying to work through the list of pit-filling requirements
jokes.punchline: Jerry has ruined something with permanent marker — again — and Leslie's response is to retroactively erase his entire existence
jokes.explanation: A reliable running gag — Jerry as the office punching bag — executed competently. 'Let's all pretend Jerry wasn't born' is a good escalation of the insult beyond the immediate situation. Standard Parks Jerry joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I panicked! I was worried he'd recognize me from the city council and ask me questions about zoning permits, so I just blurted out the first name that came to my head.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Which was?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ms. Montegue.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Where did that come from?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: Forget it. Let's all pretend Jerry wasn't born.
jokes.setup: Jerry apologizes for using permanent marker
jokes.punchline: Leslie's punishment is to collectively erase Jerry from existence — 'pretend Jerry wasn't born' is a wildly disproportionate response
jokes.explanation: The disproportionate punishment — existential erasure for using permanent marker — is delightfully cruel and very quotable. Establishes early-season Jerry abuse as a comedic institution.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This pit has been a blight on our community for far too long. But today, we rise up. Today, we take back what is ours. Today, we fill this pit.

jokes.text: Rules, codes, permits, red tape. I never realized how frustrating it is to be in the government. In my next life, I'm going into private industry. Maybe strip mining.
jokes.setup: The team is frustrated by bureaucratic obstacles to filling in the pit
jokes.punchline: Ron — a government employee and libertarian — laments being in government, then lands on 'strip mining' as his dream private sector career
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character integration. Ron's worldview — hating government while working for it, and his preference for maximally extractive industries — is summed up in a single perfect button: 'Maybe strip mining.' The setup plays into his established character contradictions. High quotability, strong economy. Comparable in quality to an 8-range anchor joke.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: You can't just play with the medical equipment!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But anything's a toy if you're brave enough.

jokes.text: Everybody take out their thinking caps. And rip them up. Then take out your doing caps, 'cause we're gonna do something today.
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to motivate her team to find a faster solution
jokes.punchline: The thinking caps/doing caps distinction is absurd but delivered with complete sincerity and Leslie's characteristic pep-talk energy
jokes.explanation: A solid Leslie moment — her motivational speeches always have this quality of sincere absurdism. 'Rip them up' before introducing doing caps is a nice structural beat. Competent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I was reading cereal boxes for entertainment.

jokes.text: I have a couple in my wallet. That's what I call condoms.
jokes.setup: Leslie says to take out thinking caps; Tom produces something from his wallet
jokes.punchline: He clarifies that he calls condoms 'thinking caps' — and then is told to focus
jokes.explanation: A predictable 'that's what I call X' joke. Tom's sexual bravado is established character territory but the wordplay here is somewhat lazy — the connection between 'thinking caps' and condoms doesn't have any particular insight. Functional but below average for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Can I smoke in your office?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What if I was already smoking when I came in?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then I would ask you to leave.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What if I was smoking a cigar, like you?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would still ask you to leave.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't even smoke. I was just curious about the rules.

jokes.text: This idea better be good. [Beat as Ann approaches]
jokes.setup: Ann has an idea to share in the meeting
jokes.punchline: Ron's pre-emptive skepticism delivered as a camera-facing aside while Ann prepares to speak
jokes.explanation: A quick deadpan beat from Ron. Economy is its strength — five words, maximum cynicism. Doesn't reach its potential but works as a Ron character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Are you on drugs?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, Ron. I'm just on the Pawnee Parks and Recreation Department.

jokes.text: I wanna move like a cheetah. Or a slug driving a remote controlled car. Something more plausible than that, but fast.
jokes.setup: Leslie says she's sick of moving slowly on the pit; she wants to move fast
jokes.punchline: Mark's suggested middle ground — a slug in a remote-controlled car — is absurd but then immediately self-corrected as 'more plausible than that'
jokes.explanation: The slug-in-remote-controlled-car image is a nice absurdist flourish. The callback to Ron's earlier remote-control play adds a layer for attentive viewers. Mark's self-correction makes it funnier — he knows it was a weird thing to say.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm going to have to write you up for the pit incident. Ka-incident.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is a ka-serious violation of department policy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You'll be receiving a ka-formal reprimand that will go in your ka-permanent file.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is no ka-joke, Leslie.

jokes.text: Would you break the rules? I won't murder.
jokes.setup: Mark asks if Leslie would break the rules to get the pit filled
jokes.punchline: Leslie's limit-setting: she'll break rules, but not commit murder — presented as a reasonable, considered position
jokes.explanation: Three words and perfect delivery. Leslie treats 'I won't murder' as a thoughtful, meaningful distinction — as if murder was actually on the table for consideration. The specificity of the negative (not 'I won't do anything illegal' but specifically 'I won't murder') is the joke. High economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ka-blam! Ka-pow! Ka-chow! You know what? Ka-SHUT THE F*** UP!

jokes.text: That's good to know.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just said 'I won't murder' as her ethical floor
jokes.punchline: Mark's completely flat 'That's good to know' treats the statement as if it were reasonable
jokes.explanation: The perfect straight-man button to the murder joke. Four words that land because of the complete absence of alarm or surprise. Works in tandem with the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I enjoy crushing people's enthusiasm. It's like a morning ritual for me.

jokes.text: You wanna get the pit filled in? Then go rent a bulldozer and fill in the freaking pit.
jokes.setup: Mark has been building toward a bold piece of advice about not asking for permission
jokes.punchline: The anticlimactic specificity of 'rent a bulldozer' — the advice is just 'literally do the thing' — delivered with exasperated directness
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the deflation of an elaborate framing ('don't ask for permission, ask for forgiveness') into the most literal possible advice. Good economy and a nice beat in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: His idea of sexy fashion is a bicep hole in a sweater

jokes.text: Say you had a friend who wanted to do something good, but a little risky, and she was kind of nervous. And this friend is me. What should I do?
jokes.setup: Leslie approaches Ann for advice, using the thin pretense of 'asking for a friend'
jokes.punchline: She immediately drops the pretense — 'and this friend is me' — before even finishing the setup, then asks directly
jokes.explanation: The 'asking for a friend' trope is well-worn, but the subversion — Leslie breaking the premise immediately — gives it a fresh Leslie-specific spin. Her inability to maintain even simple social fictions is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann was in a car accident and she's in the hospital. But here's the thing—I think this might be the universe telling us we're meant to be together. I mean, what are the odds? She crashes her car right when I'm finally ready to commit. It's like fate.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I've decided I'm going to be there for her every single day. Bring her flowers, sit by her bed, read to her. She won't be able to resist me. This is actually the best thing that could've happened to us.

jokes.text: You should do it. And ask your friend to help you because your friend totally has your back. And that friend is me.
jokes.setup: Leslie said 'this friend is me'; now Ann mirrors the same 'and that friend is me' structure
jokes.punchline: Ann echoes Leslie's awkward phrasing back at her — a mutual 'friend' callback that's both sweet and faintly absurd
jokes.explanation: A warm, gentle callback. The mirroring of Leslie's awkward phrasing is a small structural pleasure. Works as a character bonding moment with a comedic texture.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What does Mark have that I don't have?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A job.

jokes.text: What are we doing? Is it dangerous? We're not gonna murder anyone.
jokes.setup: Ann jumps in enthusiastically before knowing what they're doing
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reassurance is specifically 'we're not gonna murder anyone' — echoing her earlier line with Mark, now presented as a threshold of acceptability
jokes.explanation: The callback lands well here — 'we're not gonna murder anyone' has become Leslie's shorthand for 'this isn't TOO bad.' The escalation from personal commitment to operational briefing is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Mark has a job, a good income, a apartment, a car, maturity, and he doesn't giggle when someone says tampon.

jokes.text: I've never rented a guy before. Wish I knew about that during prom.
jokes.setup: Leslie describes how easy it was to rent a backhoe — it came with an operator ('a guy who runs it')
jokes.punchline: 'I've never rented a guy before. Wish I knew about that during prom.' — implies she didn't have a prom date and could've solved that problem by renting one
jokes.explanation: A nice piece of self-deprecating character comedy. The prom reference reveals something about Leslie's past (no date) without being pathetic — she treats it as a practical problem with a practical solution. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs. And yes, I broke some eggs today, but those eggs had it coming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, do the eggs know they had it coming? Are we asking the eggs first? Because I feel like we should be asking the eggs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, what about the chickens? Has anyone checked on the chickens?

jokes.text: There was a girl at my prom who was known as the backhoe. Mary Dunbar, she'd let anyone massage her back.
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions wishing she knew about renting a 'guy' for prom; Tom reveals he knew a girl called 'the backhoe' at his prom
jokes.punchline: The expected implication is sexual — the reveal is that she simply let people massage her back. The anti-punchline is funnier than the expected one.
jokes.explanation: A strong misdirection joke. The audience assumes 'the backhoe' is a crude sexual nickname; the reveal that it's purely literal (back massages) is the subversion. This is a clean, well-structured joke with a satisfying anti-punchline. The specificity of 'Mary Dunbar' adds comic weight.

dialogue.speaker: City Attorney
dialogue.line: I'm afraid we have a serious legal situation here. Andy Dwyer has been classified as the most dangerous man in town.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Andy? That's ridiculous. He's harmless!

dialogue.speaker: City Attorney
dialogue.line: According to the statute, anyone who has caused this much chaos unintentionally is deemed a threat to public safety.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm dangerous? That's awesome!

jokes.text: Look! I had these hard hats made. Check it out... 'kick ass'. I'll take that one.
jokes.setup: They're about to do something unauthorized and potentially illegal
jokes.punchline: Leslie has had custom hard hats made that say 'kick ass' — even in her rule-breaking, she planned branded merchandise
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in-character: Leslie's rebellious act still involves making custom branded accessories. The fact that she went to this trouble for an unauthorized operation tells us everything about her. 'I'll take that one' suggests she deliberated over which hat is most kick-ass. Strong visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: You can't say 'binder' because of the controversy...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What about 'folder'?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Also problematic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Um... 'file'?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Nope.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How about just... 'thing'?

dialogue.speaker: Lawyer
dialogue.line: Especially 'thing'. That's the worst one.

jokes.text: I didn't wanna tell him my real name, you know?
jokes.setup: The backhoe operator has addressed Leslie as 'Ms. Montegue' — an alias she gave him
jokes.punchline: Talking-head: she gave a fake name for her illicit bulldozing operation, treating it like a caper
jokes.explanation: The casual matter-of-factness of 'I didn't wanna tell him my real name, you know?' — as if this is a perfectly standard precaution for filling in a neighborhood pit — is very funny. Good economy in the confessional format.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The word 'situation' implies a situation exists.

jokes.text: First speech, easy... important moment here.
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to give a speech before the pit-filling begins
jokes.punchline: She narrates her own preparation as if coaching herself through a historic moment — talking into the void
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character beat — Leslie's tendency to treat mundane moments as historic events. Works as a setup for the actual speech.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What can I safely do?

dialogue.speaker: Scott
dialogue.line: Of all things, giving a pig is legally safe.

jokes.text: We are about to fill this hole now. Not with dirt, but with the courage of a thousand lions. And the solemn memory of all of our friends who have fallen in this cursed hole.
jokes.setup: Leslie has called for 'first speech' and is now delivering it
jokes.punchline: The speech is wildly overwrought for the act of filling in a small residential pit — 'courage of a thousand lions,' 'solemn memory,' 'cursed hole'
jokes.explanation: Leslie's tendency to over-romanticize and over-historicize small civic acts is the joke. 'The solemn memory of all our friends who have fallen in this cursed hole' — the grandiosity is finely calibrated. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I got you a little something. It's a pig stuffed animal.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks Leslie!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You could say this gift is... pretty un-be-lievable. Wait, no. You could say it's... sow-some. Actually, I need to be careful here legally, so let me just say: it's a pig.

jokes.text: What the ***? I'm okay.
jokes.setup: The backhoe dumps dirt into the pit — but Andy has apparently fallen asleep in the pit, unbeknownst to anyone
jokes.punchline: Andy's voice emerges from under the dirt — the ultimate reveal of how he ended up in the hospital
jokes.explanation: A masterfully planted payoff. The audience knew Andy slept in the pit but had forgotten it in the excitement of the unauthorized fill — then the dirt drops and his voice emerges. 'I'm okay' is the perfect beat. High impact, excellent structure, strong rewatch value. One of the episode's biggest laugh moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want to apologize, but my lawyers have instructed me to say the following: I regret any and all incidents that may or may not have occurred, depending on your definition of 'incident' and 'occurred.' I in no way admit fault, but I do acknowledge your feelings, which are valid, even though I'm not responsible for them.

jokes.text: That beeping was sure annoying, but this is even more annoying.
jokes.setup: Andy is in the hospital after being buried; a medical monitor is beeping
jokes.punchline: Andy's calm comparative complaint — the dirt was more annoying than the beeping, presented with complete equanimity
jokes.explanation: Andy's sunny obliviousness to his own near-burial is played beautifully. The comedy comes from him prioritizing the right complaint (the beeping) while utterly underselling the wrong one (being buried).

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Even acknowledging Andy was in the pit is legally problematic.

jokes.text: The monitor is not a toy, Andy. Anything is a toy if you play with it.
jokes.setup: Ann tells Andy the medical monitor is not a toy
jokes.punchline: Andy's philosophical counter: 'Anything is a toy if you play with it'
jokes.explanation: A quotable line with genuine insight beneath the absurdity. 'Anything is a toy if you play with it' has the quality of a zen koan from an idiot — it's technically true, deeply illogical, and tells you everything about Andy's worldview. Excellent economy. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, it's Leslie. I need to meet with you. It's urgent and confidential. Meet me at the old warehouse on the edge of town at midnight. Come alone. Don't tell anyone. This is very serious.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what, just call me back. My number is 555-0147.

jokes.text: Chalk that up to your concussion.
jokes.setup: Andy has just said 'anything is a toy if you play with it'
jokes.punchline: Ann attributes his philosophy not to his personality but to his head injury — deadpan diagnosis
jokes.explanation: Clean button on the previous joke. Ann's clinical deflation of Andy's philosophy works well as a two-hander. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi Andy, this is your Aunt Doris. I'm calling to let you know that your mother has passed away. She died this morning. We're all very sad. Call me back.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What?! Mom?!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just kidding! It's Leslie. But seriously, you need to call me back.

jokes.text: I moved out. I had to go back 'cause I forgot my headphones. And I laid down on this really comfy tarp. I saw an old cereal box I hadn't read before, so I must've drifted off. Next thing you know... dirt.
jokes.setup: Andy explains how he ended up in the pit when they filled it
jokes.punchline: The mundane chain of reasons (forgot headphones → comfy tarp → unread cereal box → fell asleep → buried) culminates in the single word 'dirt'
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. Andy's explanation of how he ended up buried is a masterpiece of character comedy and comedic economy. Every detail is pitch-perfect: the cereal box he 'hadn't read before' as his bedtime reading, the tarp as a comfort item, the shrug of 'next thing you know... dirt.' The pause before 'dirt' as the one-word summary of his entire catastrophe is extraordinary. Perfect Andy characterization. Easily the episode's most quotable and rewatchable moment.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Andy's like a badger. He burrows into things, makes a mess, and then disappears for a while.

jokes.text: It's like I'm lying on a cloud. This is awesome. Ann and Andy, just like old times. The pit works in mysterious ways.
jokes.setup: Andy is being treated in the hospital; Ann adjusts his hospital bed
jokes.punchline: 'The pit works in mysterious ways' — Andy's weirdly spiritual take on nearly being buried alive, as if the pit had a plan
jokes.explanation: Andy's invocation of the pit as a providential force is funny and strange. It also works as a character beat — he's genuinely glad to be back in Ann's proximity, even under these circumstances. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, I need to talk to you about something important.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh hey! Yeah, I got your message. You said you were coming over and you wanted me to be ready.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No, I just said I was stopping by—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm ready! I'm so ready!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, why are you naked?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You said to be ready! I thought you meant... you know... ready ready.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god. Put some clothes on.

jokes.text: I'm sorry about Andy, but I'm not sorry about what I did. What's my crime? I got bold? And a little negligent?
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head, having just been called into Ron's office
jokes.punchline: 'And a little negligent?' — she lists 'negligent' as if it's on par with 'bold,' a mild personality trait rather than a legal condition
jokes.explanation: 'I got bold? And a little negligent?' is a great Leslie line — she can't even muster genuine self-recrimination. The equal weighting of boldness and negligence as character traits is her signature blind spot played perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann said something really sexy to me yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I did not.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You did. You said, 'Andy, can you pick up some milk on your way home?'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... that's exactly what I said.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: In a sexy voice though.

jokes.text: Can I smoke in here? You don't smoke. Just asking if I can.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been called into Ron's office for a serious dressing-down
jokes.punchline: She asks to smoke purely for the principle of having agency — she doesn't even smoke
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'You don't smoke' to 'Just asking if I can' is a perfect encapsulation of Leslie asserting herself in a powerless situation. It's a defiant non-act. Very economical and clever.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, you are literally a naked baby. You have no idea what you're doing, you get distracted by literally anything, and you cry when things don't go your way.

jokes.text: Are you high? I'm high on kaboom!
jokes.setup: Leslie is acting erratic and defiant in Ron's office
jokes.punchline: She attributes her behavior to the Kaboom spirit — the episode's central absurd concept deployed as a defense
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Kaboom theme. Leslie treating 'kaboom spirit' as a literal intoxicant is funny and in character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't have time to get dressed. I'll just wear an apron.

dialogue.speaker: Someone
dialogue.line: Andy, that only covers the front.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Exactly. Problem solved.

jokes.text: Don't ask for permission, ask for forgiveness. That's right, you never did ask me for permission, did you? I'm sorry to burst your ka-bubble, but I just had my ass ka-handed to me by the city manager, and now this entire department is ka-screwed.
jokes.setup: Ron is dressing Leslie down for acting unilaterally; she quotes 'ask for forgiveness not permission' at him
jokes.punchline: Ron, irritated, deploys the 'ka-' prefix sarcastically: 'ka-bubble,' 'ka-handed,' 'ka-screwed' — weaponizing the episode's catchword as an insult delivery mechanism
jokes.explanation: Ron using the Kaboom prefix as a sarcastic rhetorical weapon is a brilliant piece of character writing. 'Ka-screwed' in particular is the perfect landing. This subverts the cheerful Kaboom catchword into bitter irony. Strong originality in execution, high character integration — only Ron would do this, and only when pushed past his limit. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann said she needs money because... she's starting a small business selling homemade candles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That doesn't sound like Ann at all.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, she told me in her Ann voice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You can't do impressions, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ron, I'm so, so, so sorry. What the ka-*** were you thinking?
jokes.setup: Leslie apologizes; Ron continues the ka- prefix rant
jokes.punchline: 'What the ka-*** were you thinking?' — the profanity-plus-ka is the peak of the running ka- joke
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the ka- prefix into the profanity slot is the logical peak of this running bit. 'What the ka-*** were you thinking?' is a great button. Strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You need like $100,000 to open a bank account.

jokes.text: I would prefer that she ask me for my permission so I can say no. I like saying no. It lowers their enthusiasm.
jokes.setup: Ron is in a talking-head explaining why he's upset about Leslie not asking permission
jokes.punchline: His objection isn't to her behavior per se — it's that she denied him the pleasure of saying no to her face
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's greatest Ron Swanson lines. 'I like saying no. It lowers their enthusiasm.' — this is a perfectly articulated philosophy. Ron's anti-government, anti-employee-morale worldview expressed with complete sincerity and zero self-awareness. The line has become one of Parks and Recreation's most quotable and shareable moments. Exceptional character integration — this is ONLY Ron. Compares favorably to the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? I could totally be a busker. People throw money at street performers all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Andy, you can't even play an instrument.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I could sing!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, fair point. I'd probably make like... two dollars a day. And one of those would be pity money.

jokes.text: My God, my sexy sweater! It has a hole cut out over the bicep.
jokes.setup: Ann brings Andy some clean clothes from her house
jokes.punchline: Andy's reaction to finding his 'sexy sweater' — which has a deliberate hole cut over the bicep — presented with genuine pride
jokes.explanation: The bicep-hole sweater is a great visual character joke — Andy's idea of 'sexy' is a DIY modification to reveal one muscle. His genuine delight in reuniting with this garment is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want to play professional football with no qualifications.

jokes.text: What do you... what do you think is happening right now? A tragic accident... reignited feelings you thought were long dead and we are finally back together.
jokes.setup: Ann has brought Andy clothes and is caring for him in the hospital
jokes.punchline: Andy has constructed an elaborate romantic narrative from this situation — complete with 'reignited feelings' — delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Andy's gap between reality and perception is the core of his character comedy. His narration of the situation — 'reignited feelings you thought were long dead' — is delivered with the confidence of a man who is completely, spectacularly wrong. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, we need to fill that pit soon. Because let's be honest, I'm gonna fall in there at least three more times before it's actually filled.

jokes.text: He has literally everything that you don't have: a job, a car, a steady income, an address, a second pair of shoes, table manners, the ability to say 'tampon' without giggling.
jokes.setup: Andy asks what Mark has that he doesn't have
jokes.punchline: Ann lists Mark's advantages — a list that starts with basics (job, car) but escalates to 'a second pair of shoes' and ends with 'the ability to say tampon without giggling'
jokes.explanation: A precision-crafted escalation list. 'A second pair of shoes' is the pivot point where the list shifts from adult competencies to kindergarten competencies, and 'the ability to say tampon without giggling' is a perfect button — simultaneously an insult and a character revelation about Andy. Strong structure, high quotability. Comparable to the 8.0 benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe the pit is actually being filled in. This is the best day of my life.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pinch me. Literally pinch me, because if this is a dream, I don't want to wake up.

jokes.text: Mark has his life together. [Beat] I'll get you a different nurse.
jokes.setup: Ann has just devastatingly listed all of Andy's shortcomings
jokes.punchline: The beat where Ann registers what she's said — perhaps too harshly — and then pivots to a purely logistical 'I'll get you a different nurse' as the only available exit
jokes.explanation: The perfect awkward escape. After the devastating list, Ann can't follow up emotionally — so she offers the most bureaucratically neutral possible response. The silence before the pivot is the comedy. It's also a subtle joke about her professional role — she literally controls the nursing staff as an option. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: You know, Andy, dropping that lawsuit is the smartest thing you've done. You're like a gopher.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A gopher?

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Yeah. You dig yourself into a hole, then you realize it's a bad idea, and you just... stop digging.

jokes.text: It's awful what happened to Andy. But sometimes when you make an omelet, you gotta break a few eggs. What's the alternative, no omelets at all? Who wants to live in that kind of world? Maybe birds. Then all their babies would live.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head justifying her decision that led to Andy being buried
jokes.punchline: She uses the 'break a few eggs' idiom, then genuinely interrogates who wouldn't want omelets, then arrives at 'maybe birds' — a perfectly absurdist logical spiral
jokes.explanation: One of the finest jokes in the episode and arguably one of the best in early Parks and Rec. The logical chain — omelets → who wouldn't want omelets → birds, because their eggs → their babies would live — is impeccable. The structure earns the absurdist punchline through genuine following-of-logic. Leslie's moral calculus is both self-serving and completely sincere. 'Then all their babies would live' is a transcendently funny button. Comparable to or exceeding the 9.5 anchor example in structural elegance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When you take a risk, your heart races, your palms get sweaty, there's this tingling sensation all over your body.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's what you just described.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know! It's incredible. I'm getting all tingly just thinking about it.

jokes.text: Is that all you lawyers think about? Lawsuits, and laws, and legalese?
jokes.setup: Scott warns them that Andy could sue them
jokes.punchline: Leslie is incredulous that a lawyer would think about lawsuits — the list of 'lawsuits, laws, and legalese' suggests she thinks these concerns are absurdly narrow-minded
jokes.explanation: Solid irony — Leslie being baffled that a lawyer cares about law. 'Legalese' added to the list gives it a nice rhythm. Leslie's obliviousness is the engine of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: The wholesome charity was actually an elaborate prank.

jokes.text: You can't say 'I'm sorry', or 'I apologize.' It implies guilt. Can't say 'victim'. Can't say 'unfortunate' and 'situation'. I can't say the word 'situation'? No, it implies there was a situation.
jokes.setup: Scott is coaching Leslie on what she cannot say to Andy for liability reasons
jokes.punchline: The escalation of forbidden words reaches the point where she can't say 'situation' because it implies there was one — the legal caution has become self-parodying
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully structured escalation. The escalation from 'don't say sorry' to 'don't say victim' to 'don't say situation' moves from recognizable legal caution to absurdist Catch-22 territory. The logic is internally consistent which makes it funnier. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: My prank philosophy is simple: I identify something that will cause maximum chaos and confusion, then I execute it flawlessly.

dialogue.speaker: Keith
dialogue.line: For my next prank, I'm going to build a community center in the South Side. They've needed one for years.

jokes.text: Can I give him the pig? Pig's fine.
jokes.setup: Everything Leslie could possibly say is legally forbidden
jokes.punchline: She resorts to offering a stuffed pig instead of words — and Scott clears this as legally permissible
jokes.explanation: After the escalating list of forbidden words, Leslie's solution — a stuffed pig — is brilliant. The attorney's calm 'Pig's fine' is the perfect straight-man response. 'Pig's fine' is one of the best two-word punchlines in the episode. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: Hope you squeal better.
jokes.setup: Leslie hands Andy a stuffed pig as a get-well gift
jokes.punchline: 'Hope you squeal better' — a pig-based pun on 'feel better'
jokes.explanation: A clean, well-executed pun. 'Squeal' for 'feel' is simple but effective. Leslie's delivery of a pre-planned pun that avoids all liability is a nice character beat — she worked out something to say that's legally permissible and still warm.

jokes.text: Leslie brings Andy a stuffed pig. Lawyer: 'Pig's fine.' Leslie to Andy: 'Got this for you. Hope you squeal better.'
jokes.setup: Leslie can't say any normal words of comfort due to legal restrictions, but she can give a gift.
jokes.punchline: Her alternative to 'I hope you feel better' is 'I hope you squeal better' — a pig-themed pun that technically avoids all the banned phrases while still communicating sympathy.
jokes.explanation: Sharp pun with excellent structural setup. The legal restriction scene exists partly to set up this payoff — Leslie's solution to 'can't express sympathy verbally' is to bring a pig and use a pig pun. Clean, well-constructed joke.

jokes.text: Andy, I just wanted to say, I am so, so, so... filled... with emotions. As any person would.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to express genuine remorse but cannot say 'sorry' or 'apologize' per the attorney
jokes.punchline: She becomes pathetically verbal in her evasion: 'filled... with emotions. As any person would.'
jokes.explanation: The execution of the 'no forbidden words' constraint lands beautifully here. 'Filled with emotions. As any person would.' manages to be both a failed apology and an inadvertent non-apology masterpiece. The pause before 'filled' shows Leslie mid-edit, which is the cringe comedy working perfectly.

jokes.text: No miming. You were in the pit. We're not conceding that point. You were in a place... we're both here now. The government... We gotta go.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to communicate with Andy but every option is legally blocked, including apparently physical gestures
jokes.punchline: The attorney cuts her off at every turn — even 'in the pit' has to become 'in a place' — until the only option is to leave
jokes.explanation: The running legal censorship reaches a satisfying comedic peak. 'No miming' is a great surprise escalation — the prohibition has now extended beyond words. 'We gotta go' as the only legally safe exit is a perfect button on the bit.

jokes.text: Andy, it's Leslie. Hello. Andy, it's Leslie. Psych! Leave a message after the beep.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Andy and gets his voicemail
jokes.punchline: Andy's voicemail greeting says his name twice as if answering, then 'Psych!' — a classic fake-out still apparently used by Andy as an adult man
jokes.explanation: A perfect Andy character joke — the 'Psych!' voicemail prank is something a 12-year-old would do. The joke is that he still thinks it's brilliant. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hey, Andy, it's your aunt. Your mom or dad's sister. I don't know how to tell you this, but... your uncle has passed. He's with Jesus now. So we're having a memorial in 30 minutes at city hall.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying increasingly desperate tactics to get Andy to come to city hall
jokes.punchline: She pretends to be his aunt, kills off an uncle, and holds a fake memorial to lure him out — the qualifier 'your mom or dad's sister' shows she's overexplaining the cover story
jokes.explanation: The parenthetical definition of 'aunt' — 'your mom or dad's sister' — is the funniest word in this joke. Leslie is so desperate she's explaining family relationships in her fake cover story, as if Andy needs clarification on what an aunt is. Dark and funny.

jokes.text: Hey, free guitars at city hall! Everybody run!
jokes.setup: Leslie is leaving increasingly unhinged messages trying to lure Andy to city hall
jokes.punchline: She pivots from fake death to free guitars — knowing Andy is a musician, this is her most targeted (and most absurd) lure
jokes.explanation: 'Everybody run!' is a great touch — she's broadcasting a fake event to the general public in her desperation. The pivot from fake uncle death to 'free guitars' is a perfectly calibrated escalation of absurdity.

jokes.text: That was weird. How long have you been there?
jokes.setup: Leslie has been leaving increasingly unhinged voicemails — apparently while Ann was present and watching
jokes.punchline: Ann's reaction implies she witnessed the entire escalating performance without intervening
jokes.explanation: A competent reaction beat — the comedy is Ann's presumably horrified witnessing of the voicemail series. Economy is good; doesn't add much beyond a grace note on the previous sequence.

jokes.text: Leslie, the man lived in a pit. He couldn't find a place to live on the earth's surface, so he went under the ground. You're dealing with a grown man who thinks like a gopher.
jokes.setup: Leslie insists Andy isn't suing just for the money
jokes.punchline: 'You're dealing with a grown man who thinks like a gopher' — Ann's clinically accurate characterization of Andy's decision-making capacity
jokes.explanation: Excellent. The buildup — 'couldn't find a place to live on the earth's surface, so he went under the ground' — earns the punchline 'thinks like a gopher.' This is Ann's most cutting and accurate read of Andy. High quotability, strong structure, good character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: Baby, I'm back. Thank you so... Why are you naked? Because of what you said, we're getting back together.
jokes.setup: Ann has called Andy to talk privately; he shows up naked
jokes.punchline: Andy has interpreted 'can we talk at my house?' as an invitation to arrive already naked for their reunion
jokes.explanation: A classic Andy misreading of social signals, escalated to a visual extreme. The confidence with which he arrives naked based on a completely neutral phone call is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: You should've heard the sexy stuff she said. I said 'hey, Andy, it's Ann, can we talk at my house?' That's not how you said it, you were like, 'Hey, Andy, it's Ann, can you talk at my house?'
jokes.setup: Andy claims Ann said something sexy; Ann quotes exactly what she said
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'correction' — emphasizing the italics on 'you' — presents a completely identical sentence as fundamentally different in meaning and seductive intent
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke. The humor depends entirely on the performance — Andy's earnest emphasis on 'you' as if it transforms the sentence into an invitation. This is a joke that reveals character (Andy's capacity for wish-fulfillment perception), has perfect economy, and is rooted in the specificity of the actual words spoken. One of the episode's strongest jokes. The word 'you' doing all the comedic work is exceptional writing.

jokes.text: My God, you're such a baby. Literally. Big naked baby, put clothes on.
jokes.setup: Andy shows up naked; Ann criticizes him
jokes.punchline: She calls him a baby, then literally means it — 'literally. Big naked baby.'
jokes.explanation: The literal/figurative double meaning of 'baby' is a quick, clean joke. 'Big naked baby' as a description is vivid and funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: Has he showed up naked before? Anniversaries, birthdays, holidays.
jokes.setup: Leslie, seeing Andy has arrived naked, asks if this has happened before
jokes.punchline: Ann's matter-of-fact list of occasions — 'anniversaries, birthdays, holidays' — establishes this as a recurring pattern
jokes.explanation: Ann's weary three-item list is perfectly economical. The punchline is the exhausted resignation with which she identifies the pattern. Very good economy.

jokes.text: Is she gone?
jokes.setup: Leslie has left after realizing Andy is naked
jokes.punchline: Andy waits for Leslie to leave before proceeding with the conversation — still wearing nothing but an apron
jokes.explanation: A quick reaction beat. Andy treating Leslie's departure as a privacy prerequisite for his naked conversation is funny in context. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: None of your clothes fit me, so I'm putting an apron over the front stuff.
jokes.setup: Andy needs to get dressed but Ann's clothes don't fit him
jokes.punchline: 'The front stuff' — Andy's euphemism — and the solution of an apron as clothing
jokes.explanation: 'The front stuff' is a perfectly Andy euphemism — childlike, squeamish, somehow both crude and innocent. The apron solution is visually absurd and perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I want Ann back, and she said she needs a guy with a lot of money. That doesn't sound like Ann. I can't really do her voice.
jokes.setup: Andy explains why he decided to sue — Ann supposedly told him she needs a rich man
jokes.punchline: Leslie skeptically says that doesn't sound like Ann; Andy's reply — 'I can't really do her voice' — is a perfect non-sequitur that reveals he's been doing an impression in his head, not quoting
jokes.explanation: Outstanding. 'I can't really do her voice' is one of the sharpest lines in the episode. It retroactively recontextualizes Andy's entire explanation — he's been narrating an internal fantasy, not reporting actual events. The admission reveals not just that he's wrong, but that he knew he was doing a voice impression of Ann in his own head. Perfect economy, exceptional character integration, very high quotability.

jokes.text: Sometimes I think the right thing to do is to not take shortcuts. I tried to fill in the pit. That didn't work either. Fine. I'll get a job. Ann will respect that. I can make six bucks a day playing guitar in the street. I can't make six bucks a day.
jokes.setup: Andy reflects on shortcuts and decides to go legitimate — then immediately calculates his income from street guitar
jokes.punchline: He estimates six dollars a day as a viable income, then immediately contradicts himself: 'I can't make six bucks a day'
jokes.explanation: Andy's self-correction in real time — 'I can make six bucks a day... I can't make six bucks a day' — is a great beat. The fact that six dollars is his income ceiling AND he can't reach it tells you everything about his financial situation. Strong character comedy with good structure.

jokes.text: Wait a second. I know I just said that shortcuts are bad, but I kind of just thought of an awesome shortcut.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just given Andy a speech about not taking shortcuts
jokes.punchline: She immediately pivots to proposing a shortcut — her principles lasted about thirty seconds
jokes.explanation: Good self-aware character comedy. Leslie's inability to resist a scheme even when she just condemned schemes is true to her. The phrasing 'kind of just thought of an awesome shortcut' is good.

jokes.text: Never, I will not negotiate with greedy street people.
jokes.setup: Leslie brings Andy to negotiate dropping the lawsuit; Ron refuses before hearing terms
jokes.punchline: Ron characterizes Andy — a man in a hospital gown / apron — as 'greedy street people'
jokes.explanation: Ron's contemptuous refusal and the categorization of Andy as 'greedy street people' is great Ron Swanson character comedy. The phrase treats Andy as a street-level extortionist rather than an injured neighbor, which somehow fits.

jokes.text: A guaranteed starting spot on the Indianapolis Colts... inside linebacker. We can't accomplish that.
jokes.setup: Andy has a second condition after his reasonable first one
jokes.punchline: He wants a starting NFL position — on a specific team, at a specific position — as part of a city government settlement
jokes.explanation: The specificity — Indianapolis Colts, inside linebacker — makes this much funnier than a generic 'I want to be on a sports team.' Andy has thought about this specific position. Ron's flat 'We can't accomplish that' is the perfect nonplussed response.

jokes.text: I think that Andy seems like he doesn't care so much about the second one. And he would be fine with us just filling in the pit.
jokes.setup: Andy has made the NFL demand but his body language suggests it's not serious
jokes.punchline: Leslie narrates Andy's apparent priorities to Ron as if reading his mind — and she's right
jokes.explanation: Leslie's cheerful translation of Andy's nonverbal communication into a settlement strategy is funny in context. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I've already been injured in that thing twice. And I can fall in ten more times by 'eventually'. Every time I walk past that pit, I'm forced to relive the most traumatic two separate days of my life and wanna sue you again.
jokes.setup: Ron says the pit will 'eventually' be filled; Andy objects
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'ten more times' escalation, and especially 'the most traumatic two separate days' — acknowledging both pit incidents with the specificity of 'two separate days'
jokes.explanation: Andy's legal argument — that he could fall in ten more times — is delivered with genuine sincerity. 'The most traumatic two separate days' acknowledges the absurdity of having two separate pit traumas while treating it with appropriate gravity. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Usually in these situations a person says 'pinch me.'
jokes.setup: The settlement is happening — the pit will be filled; Leslie can barely believe it worked
jokes.punchline: She references the 'pinch me' convention while not actually asking to be pinched — observing the tradition while maintaining decorum
jokes.explanation: Weak end to an otherwise strong sequence. The joke is too mild and doesn't add much. Leslie's excitement deserved a stronger button here.

jokes.text: Just one of his conditions for the settlement, I guess. He settled? Gave up $100,000 probably. Just for one thing. The city fill in the pit behind your house. Why? Who knows? Who knows why that gopher does what he does?
jokes.setup: Ann is shocked Andy dropped the lawsuit for just the pit being filled
jokes.punchline: Mark reprises 'gopher' — now a shared reference for Andy's incomprehensible animal logic
jokes.explanation: A good callback to Ann's 'gopher' line — now Mark uses it as shared vocabulary. 'Who knows why that gopher does what he does?' is a great extension of the metaphor. Effective structural callback.

jokes.text: Good-bye, pit... hello, lot.
jokes.setup: The pit is being filled and Leslie watches the transformation
jokes.punchline: Her farewell to the pit and hello to the lot — the anticlimactic upgrade of 'pit' to 'lot' as the triumphant conclusion
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. The parallelism of 'goodbye pit / hello lot' is a perfect encapsulation of civic progress in its most modest form. An empty lot is not an inspiring victory, but Leslie delivers it as if it were. The line works as character comedy and as a genuine moment of Leslie-style optimism.

jokes.text: How does taking risks make me feel? Amazing. Tingling sensation throughout my whole body. I feel flushed. My muscles feel relaxed, yet I feel awake. Just waves of pleasure. I wish there was something physical that can make me feel this way.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking-head reflecting on the episode's events
jokes.punchline: Her description of the 'risk high' is an obvious metaphor for sexual arousal — 'tingling,' 'flushed,' 'waves of pleasure' — ending with 'I wish there was something physical that could make me feel this way'
jokes.explanation: A sophisticated and well-constructed talking-head joke. Leslie is oblivious to the obvious subtext of her own description. The final line — 'I wish there was something physical that could make me feel this way' — is the perfect button, delivered without any awareness. Strong character integration and a longer escalation structure that pays off well.

jokes.text: You did it. You thinking what I'm thinking? There's so much more to do. We're so close!
jokes.setup: The pit is filled; Ann thinks they're celebrating the end
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately pivots to the next project — the empty lot needs to become a playground; Ann's 'we're so close' is ironic given they're at square one for the next phase
jokes.explanation: A competent scene beat that establishes ongoing plot momentum. The comedy is mild — Leslie's indefatigable ambition — but doesn't land as a strong standalone joke.

jokes.text: I'm gonna call kaboom! and check on their availability for next year. Great. Information. Hi, I'd like the number for kaboom! The national playground building charity. I hope they can work us in.
jokes.setup: Leslie wants to call Kaboom! to plan a playground build
jokes.punchline: She calls directory assistance — not recognizing that Kaboom! operates differently — setting up the reveal
jokes.explanation: Setup for the episode's final reveal. Functions as necessary scaffolding for joke 90, the cold close punchline.

jokes.text: Sorry, there's no listing for that name. What? Are you sure? Kaboom! Is a word I made up. It's not in any dictionary. I trick people into building playgrounds in empty lots in their neighborhood. It's an elaborate prank. For my next prank, I'm gonna build a hospital in a poor part of China. They'll never see it coming!
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to look up Kaboom! — it doesn't exist in the phone directory. Then Keith appears in a talking head to explain why.
jokes.punchline: Kaboom! is a made-up word Keith uses to trick people into doing community service — and his 'next prank' is building a hospital in China. The whole episode's premise is revealed as a charitable con.
jokes.explanation: A masterful cold close. The reveal that Kaboom! is an 'elaborate prank' of tricking people into doing good works is inspired — it subverts the entire episode's optimistic energy while keeping it warm. Then the escalation to building a hospital in China, with 'they'll never see it coming,' is perfectly absurd and dark. The episode's best structural joke: it recontextualizes everything. One of the best tag-scene jokes in early Parks and Rec.

jokes.text: Kaboom! is a word I made up. It's not in any dictionary. I trick people into building playgrounds in empty lots in their neighborhood. It's an elaborate prank. For my next prank, I'm gonna build a hospital in a poor part of China. They'll never see it coming!
jokes.setup: Kaboom! turns out to have no official existence
jokes.punchline: Keith reveals the entire organization is an elaborate prank — and his next 'prank' is building a hospital for the poor in China
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a perfect closer. The reveal that Kaboom! is an 'elaborate prank' that tricks people into doing genuine good for their communities is a beautiful subversion — it's not malicious, it's altruistic lunacy. 'They'll never see it coming!' applied to building a hospital for the poor is inspired — it reframes genuine charity as a comic heist. The structure is perfect: entire episode builds to this punchline. Keith's smiling, oblivious sincerity ('they'll never see it coming!') is the definitive Parks and Rec comic spirit — optimism through absurdism. Comparable to the top calibration anchors. Fully justifies 9+ craft score.

tmdb_overview: Leslie, Ann and the rest of the Parks Department volunteer to help the organization KaBOOM! build a playground for a neighboring town. After building an entire playground in one day, Leslie gets frustrated at the lack of progress with the pit, and takes some advice from Mark to cut through the red tape.
insight: Early Season 2 stumbles with 59 jokes at moderate density but minimal standout moments.
